Negligent

/NEG-lih-juhnt/ - the stress falls on NEG · adjective

Hear It

What It Means

Negligent means habitually careless; failing to take proper care.

A negligent pharmacist left the vaccine cooler unplugged through two summer weekends in a row.

Worked Example

The server farm's night technician had one job list: check the backup drives, rotate the tapes, note the temperatures. What happened instead ran on from March to September — boxes ticked without a single tape rotated, alerts clicked away unread, spare drives never bought. When the main drive died, there was nothing behind it.

Negligent is the exact word for that technician, because negligent means habitually careless, failing to take proper care — the duty was his, and the lapse ran on for half a year. Careless is one dropped stitch; negligent is a pattern of them, in work someone was trusted to do.

Compare the words

Synonyms · words with a similar meaning

careless: one slip can be careless; negligent is a habit of slips

sloppy: untidy in the doing — duty or no duty

What it isn’t · antonyms and near-opposites

careful: taking the trouble the job requires

attentive: watching for what could go wrong

Where it sits · how deep the disregard for safety runs — careless → negligent → reckless

careless vs. negligent: Careless covers a single slip — one forgotten email, one unchecked box, shrugged off by lunchtime.

reckless vs. negligent: Reckless goes further than negligent — the negligent driver never checks the mirrors, while the reckless one sees the ice and speeds up anyway.

Build the Word

The pieces

Prefix — neg

Prefix — neg: not (Latin nec-)

Root — lig

Root — lig: to pick up, to gather (Latin legere)

Suffix — -ent

Suffix — -ent: adjective ending

Put it together

Put it together: Neg (not) + lig (to pick up) + -ent = not picking things up. Latin neglegere was literally to leave something ungathered — mail unopened, warnings unread, duties left lying where they fell. The word's picture is exact: care is a thing you pick up, and the negligent person walks past it.

Use the root in a new word: eligible

Use the root in a new word: eligible: Players eligible for the draft can be picked up — the same root legere, choosing and gathering, with a hopeful e- in front.

Root Check

Word Choice

critical / formal

Negligent is the odd one out in this unit: it names a failure of care, not a form of it. Courts reach for it when a duty existed and nobody met it. Keep it clear of lenient — a lenient judge chooses mildness on purpose, while a negligent one has stopped paying attention — and of docile, which is about being easily led, not failing anyone.
